abstract: Gad Levanon of the Burning Glass Institute argues that the widely reported weak US labor market is really two labor markets, and that the weakness sits almost entirely on the credentialed side. He ranks each demographic and occupational group's 12-month moving-average unemployment rate as a percentile against that same group's own history back to 2003, which controls for the fact that different groups have structurally different unemployment levels. On that basis the 88 million workers aged 22 and over without a bachelor's degree, more than half the labor force, sit near the strongest readings of the past twenty years, while degree-holders have deteriorated. The sharpest illustration is within the same age band: young college graduates aged 22-34 sit at the 70th percentile of their own history while young non-graduates of the same age sit at the 25th. Those two series tracked each other for two decades and decoupled in 2024. The same split runs through occupations and geography: blue-collar and manual-service workers (65 million) sit at the 18th percentile; STEM is the only occupational group above its own median; non-metro areas sit at the 12th percentile while the top 50 metros climbed roughly 30 percentile points; 47 of 51 jurisdictions sit below their own median. Levanon explicitly names two non-AI explanations for non-graduate strength: immigration enforcement shrinking labor supply in the occupations these workers hold, and a construction and data-center building boom raising demand for them.
keyFindings: The 88 million US workers aged 22+ without a bachelor's degree, more than half the labor force, sit near their best unemployment readings in twenty years.

Within the same age band, young college graduates aged 22-34 sit at the 70th percentile of their own history since 2003 while young non-graduates sit at the 25th; the two series decoupled in 2024 after moving together for two decades.
Young college graduates are roughly 20 million workers, about one in eight in the labor force, which is why their deterioration dominates coverage of an otherwise mixed market.
Blue-collar and manual-service workers (65 million) sit at the 18th percentile of their own history; STEM is the only occupational group above its own median.
Non-metro areas sit at the 12th percentile of their own history while the top 50 metropolitan areas climbed roughly 30 percentile points; 47 of 51 jurisdictions sit below their own median.
Levanon names immigration enforcement (shrinking labor supply) and the construction and data-center building boom (raising labor demand) as non-AI drivers of non-graduate strength.
methodology: Unemployment rates by educational attainment, age, occupation group and geography from BLS/CPS, smoothed as 12-month moving averages and then converted to percentile ranks against each group's own distribution since 2003. Percentile ranking is the central methodological choice: it makes groups with structurally different unemployment levels comparable by asking how each is doing relative to its own norm rather than against a common rate. One month was interpolated to cover the October 2025 federal shutdown gap in CPS collection.
qualifiers: Every headline figure is a percentile rank against a group's own history, not an unemployment rate, so the numbers cannot be read as levels or differenced against rate-denominated series. The raw rates that are given (6.4% for dropouts, 2.5% for advanced-degree holders) are not AI-attributed. The article makes no causal claim that AI drives the graduate/non-graduate divergence, and Levanon himself offers two competing explanations for the non-graduate side (immigration enforcement, construction and data-center demand) that are unrelated to AI. Percentile ranking also compresses magnitude: a group can sit at a low percentile while its absolute rate remains high, and vice versa. Self-published LinkedIn newsletter rather than a peer-reviewed or institutionally released paper, though it reflects Burning Glass Institute analysis and follows the same method as Levanon's earlier education-penalty work.
